newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt under mounting pressure over media.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt under mounting pressure over media.

text.p: The Australian government came under mounting pressure on Monday not to ease media ownership limits, with one party threatening a parliamentary inquiry and a public appeal to the prime minister from leading Australians.

Cheryl Kernot, who heads the influential minor party, The Australian Democrats, said she increasingly supported a parliamentary inquiry into any changes to media cross-ownership laws. "I am firming up in my views that we may need to have an opportunity to ask the appropriate questions," Kernot told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"The events of the past few days lead me to conclude that we might have to move sooner rather than later," Kernot said.
Liberal Prime Minister John Howard has indicated a review of ownership rules may lead to an easing of restrictions limiting cross-holdings in newspapers and electronic media.
Cabinet is expected to consider media ownership this week.
The existing rules set up by the former Labor government prevent a television station from holding more than 15 percent of a major newspaper in the same market, and vice versa.

Television boss Kerry Stokes has accused Howard of striking a deal with Australia's richest man, television and magazine tycoon Kerry Packer, to deliver control of a major newspaper company, John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, in exchange for political support. Howard has denied the claim.

As the government considers its position, about 80 prominent politicians, artists, clergy and other community leaders -- including former Liberal prime minister Malcolm Fraser -- on Monday published an open plea to Howard to ensure ownership remained as diverse and independent as possible.
"We urge you not to allow media ownership to fall into fewer hands," they wrote in a letter to Howard.
"The ownership of Australia's newspapers, television and radio stations is already among the most concentrated in the world," the letter said.
"Whatever the difficulties these (existing) rules present, they have worked as a minimum guarantee of diversity."

The current restrictions prevent Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd from increasing its 15 percent Fairfax stake and taking over the company, which publishes leading broadsheets and a national financial daily.

The allegation by Stokes, chairman of the Seven Network Ltd, arose after a report in the Fairfax-owned Australian Financial Review that Howard had tried to broker an arrangement wherby Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd could raise its Seven stake if News backed an easing of ownership limits to allow Packer to take over Fairfax.
Kernot, a signatory of the letter to Howard, said the government must publicly explain any change to the laws.
"The bottom line is ... that you should be willing to make the case for change publicly," she said.
"Media ownership is not the gift of prime ministers, or shouldn't be the gift of primse ministers to bestow as favours in return for favourable publicity," she said.

"It would be good to have an opportunity to test what's been said already -- did John Howard really offer some kind of trade off to keep not just one media baron but the two most important ones in this country happy."
The Democrats will on Tuesday consider their position on an inquiry by parliament's upper house, the Senate.
They would need the support of the Labor opposition, other minority parties and independents to force an inquiry against the government's wishes.
